content: A palindrome is a sequence of characters, such as a word, phrase, number, or other arrangement, that reads identically forward and backward. This definition typically allows for the adjustment of punctuation, spaces, and capitalization. The term palindrome originates from the Greek words palin, meaning back, and dromos, meaning way or direction. The English writer Ben Jonson coined the term in the 1600s. In ancient Greek, the phenomenon was referred to as karkinikê epigrafê, or crab inscription, symbolizing the backward movement of crabs, akin to the reversible nature of palindromes. Historical Examples of Palindromes Palindromes have been documented as far back as 79 A.D. One of the earliest examples is the Latin word square Sator Arepo Tenet Opera Rotas, discovered as graffiti in Herculaneum, a city buried by volcanic ash. This palindrome is unique because it forms a word square that can be read in multiple directions: horizontally, vertically, and even in reverse. While some interpret it as The sower Arepo holds the wheels at work, the exact meaning remains unclear, as Arepo is not a known Latin word. Some scholars suggest it may have been a coded Christian symbol, with the word TENET forming a cross. Another notable palindrome is a Hebrew example by the medieval scholar Ibn Ezra: We explained the glutton who is in the honey was burned and incinerated. This palindrome addresses a halachic (Jewish legal) question about whether honey becomes non-kosher if a fly lands in it. In Latin, the palindrome In girum imus nocte et consumimur igni translates to We go wandering at night and are consumed by fire, likely describing the behavior of moths. This phrase is thought to originate from medieval times. Byzantine Greeks often inscribed the palindrome Wash my sins, not only my face (Νίψον ἀνομήματα μὴ μόναν ὄψιν) on baptismal fonts. This inscription can be found in various historical locations, including St. Mary’s Church in Nottingham, the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, and several churches across Europe. Palindromes in Ancient Sanskrit Sanskrit poetry from ancient India explored palindromes of remarkable complexity. One of the most intricate examples appears in the 19th canto of the 8th-century epic poem Śiśupāla-vadha by Magha. This palindrome can be read forwards, backwards, upwards, and downwards, showcasing an extraordinary level of linguistic and poetic skill. Types of Palindromes Character-Based Palindromes The most common type of palindrome involves individual characters. Examples in English include words like civic, level, rotor, kayak, and racecar. Palindromic phrases and sentences also exist, such as Was it a rat I saw? and Step on no pets. In these cases, punctuation, capitalization, and spacing are often disregarded. Famous English palindromes include Able was I ere I saw Elba, A man, a plan, a canal, Panama. and Madam, I'm Adam. Word-Based Palindromes Some palindromes use entire words as units rather than individual letters. Examples include Fall leaves after leaves fall and First Ladies rule the State and state the rule: ladies first. These palindromes maintain symmetry at the word level. Line-Based Palindromes Certain palindromes operate at the level of entire lines. For instance, James A. Lindon’s poem Doppelganger and the dialogue Crab Canon in Douglas Hofstadter’s Gödel, Escher, Bach are structured as line-by-line palindromes. In the latter, the second half of the dialogue mirrors the first half, with characters reversing roles. Palindromes in Molecular Biology In molecular biology, palindromic sequences are found in DNA. These sequences are symmetrical, meaning they read the same on one strand as on the complementary strand when reversed. For example, the DNA sequence ACCTAGGT is palindromic because its complementary strand, TGGATCCA, mirrors it. Palindromic DNA sequences can form hairpin structures and are often recognized by restriction enzymes, which cut DNA at specific sites. Palindromes are also prevalent in bacterial genomes and may play a role in genetic repair mechanisms, such as those observed in the Y chromosome. Palindromic Numbers A palindromic number is a numerical sequence that reads the same forwards and backwards, such as 121 or 58285. These numbers are studied in recreational mathematics, and some, like palindromic primes, hold special properties. Palindromic Dates Dates can also be palindromic, depending on the format used. For example, February 20, 2002, written as 20-02-2002 in the dd/mm/yyyy format, is a palindrome. Such dates often attract interest from numerologists and the general public. Palindromes in Music Musical compositions have also employed palindromic structures. Joseph Haydn’s Symphony No. 47 in G, nicknamed The Palindrome, features a third movement that is symmetrical. Alban Berg’s opera Lulu includes a palindromic interlude, and Béla Bartók frequently used palindromic forms in his works. Anton Webern, influenced by Renaissance composer Heinrich Isaac, incorporated both horizontal and vertical symmetries in his compositions, such as the second movement of his Opus 27 Piano Variations. Acoustic Palindromes An acoustic palindrome occurs when a recorded phrase sounds the same when played backward. Composer John Oswald discovered this phenomenon in 1974 while working with audio recordings of William S. Burroughs. Long Palindromes Single Words The longest palindromic word in the Oxford English Dictionary is tattarrattat, coined by James Joyce in Ulysses to mimic the sound of a knock on a door. Other examples include detartrated (a chemical term) and rotavator (a type of agricultural machine). The Finnish word saippuakivikauppias (soapstone vendor) is considered the longest palindromic word in everyday use. Biological Structures In genetics, palindromic sequences are common in DNA and proteins. These sequences may play roles in structural stability, protein interactions, or the formation of low-complexity regions. On the Y chromosome, palindromic arrangements allow for self-repair by folding at the midpoint. Computation Theory In computational theory, the set of all palindromes in a given alphabet is context-free but not regular. This means that a finite-state machine cannot reliably identify palindromes, especially for long sequences. Testing for palindromes requires reading the entire sequence to locate the midpoint. Semordnilaps A semordnilap is a word or phrase that forms a different word or phrase when reversed. For example, stressed becomes desserts, and diaper becomes repaid. The term semordnilap itself is palindromes spelled backward. Non-English Palindromes Palindromes exist in many languages, including those with non-alphabetic writing systems. In Chinese, for instance, palindromes are based on characters that represent words rather than letters. The treatment of diacritics varies by language, with some preserving palindromes regardless of accents. Examples of English Palindromes Step on no pets Dammit, I’m mad. Rise to vote, sir Never odd or even Yo, banana boy. Do geese see God? No lemon, no melon Was it a car or a cat I saw? Family-Related Palindromes Many familial nicknames are palindromes, such as Mom, Dad, Pop, and Sis. Variations like Momma, Poppa, and Nanna also exhibit this symmetry. The term Abba, used to refer to God the Father, is another example.
